title: Direct Tempering Effects on Microstructure and Mechanical Properties in Laser-Based DED AISI 431 Martensitic Stainless Steel
abstract: Abstract Post-build tempering response was investigated for AISI Type 431 martensitic stainless steel produced via laser-based Directed Energy Deposition (DED-LB) at 350-650 °C. Phase evolution and stored strain were quantified using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and x-ray diffraction (XRD) with Rietveld refinement, then correlated with hardness and build-oriented tensile properties. A wrought AISI Type 431 hardened-and-tempered bar served as a benchmark reference. The as-deposited DED-LB microstructure comprised highly strained lath martensite containing δ-ferrite pockets, retained austenite, and Si-Mn-rich oxide inclusions inherited from the water-atomized feedstock, resulting in inherently brittle mechanical behavior. A low-temperature austenite reversion window was identified, with austenite peaking at approximately 6.7% following tempering at 350 °C and preferentially nucleating at δ-ferrite/martensite interfaces. This condition produced a substantial ductility increase, with elongation rising from 1.2% in the as-deposited state to 10.2% while sustaining tensile strength above 1180 MPa. Tempering at 450 °C induced secondary hardening, achieving a peak hardness of 606 HV5, accompanied by reduced elongation as austenite content declined. Above 550 °C, austenite decreased below 1%, transitioning toward a predominantly tempered martensitic microstructure and wrought-like ductility. The ductility evolution across the tempering series is governed by matrix recovery rather than inclusion content. The austenitization-free, single-step tempering route provides a systematic and industry-relevant thermal processing strategy for tailoring strength–ductility trade-offs and mitigating build-induced residual strain sensitivity in additively manufactured martensitic stainless steels. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Martensitic stainless steels were developed to provide a corrosion-resistant alloy system capable of being strengthened by martensitic transformation and subsequent tempering, in contrast to the solution-strengthened austenitic grades. By combining moderate chromium levels with controlled carbon content, these alloys achieve high hardness and strength while retaining useful resistance to atmospheric and mildly aggressive environments. AISI Type 431 (≈15-17% Cr, 1.25-2.5% Ni, ≤ 0.20% C) exemplifies this class and is conventionally employed in a quenched-and-tempered condition for shafts, fasteners, valve stems, and other components subjected to combined mechanical loading and corrosion exposure (Ref  1 ,  2 ). Interest in this alloy has recently extended to additive manufacturing (AM), particularly laser-based Directed Energy Deposition (DED-LB), where its property balance is attractive for repair, restoration, and near-net-shape fabrication of steel components (Ref  3 ,  4 ).

DED-LB, however, fundamentally alters the microstructural state relative to wrought processing. Layer-by-layer deposition subjects the material to repeated, highly non-isothermal thermal cycles that promote solidification texture, microstructural gradients, elevated dislocation densities, and substantial residual stresses (Ref  5 ,  6 ). In martensitic alloys, this can produce an as-deposited condition characterized by retained δ-ferrite, high transformation-induced strain, and austenite fractions substantially exceeding those typical of conventionally quenched-and-tempered wrought products (Ref  7 ,  8 - 9 ). XRD-Rietveld analyses of DED-LB Type 420 stainless steel have reported phase mixtures containing ~ 23% δ-ferrite and ~ 29% retained austenite under non-preheated build conditions, with retained austenite levels also reported around ~ 22 wt.% in comparable DED builds (Ref  10 ,  11 ). The result is high as-deposited hardness but inherently limited ductility and increased property scatter (Ref  12 ,  13 ). Post-build heat treatment, therefore, becomes appealing to stabilize the phase constitution, relax stored strain, and restore mechanical performance suitable for structural service.

Conventional heat treatment of wrought AISI Type 431 prescribes austenitization, quench, and subsequent tempering to achieve the target strength–toughness balance. This sequence is poorly suited to DED-LB components. High-temperature austenitization and rapid quenching introduce residual-stress, distortion, and cracking susceptibility that are difficult to manage in large, geometrically complex, or substrate-bonded builds (Ref  14 ). These constraints are particularly acute in the repair and cladding applications that dominate industrial DED-LB use, where thermal processing must respect deposit–substrate integrity and component geometry (Ref  4 ,  15 ). Substrate preheating can reduce thermal gradients and mitigate cracking during deposition (Ref  16 ,  17 ), and post-build treatments are known to substantially modify hardness, wear response, and retained austenite evolution in laser-deposited steels (Ref  18 ,  19 ). Yet, the inherited wrought heat treatment prescription does not account for the AM microstructural state. A simplified route that tempers directly from the as-deposited condition, bypassing austenitization entirely, is therefore industrially attractive.

Prior work confirms that laser-deposited martensitic stainless steels are strongly sensitive to post-build thermal processing, with the as-deposited microstructure and defect state conditioning the mechanisms activated during heat treatment. DED-LB AISI Type 410 exhibits high as-deposited hardness with limited elongation, followed by progressive strength loss at elevated tempering temperatures as carbide coarsening progresses (Ref  12 ). Laser-deposited AISI Type 431 material shows process-dependent phase balance governed by local cooling rate and solidification conditions (Ref  7 ,  9 ). Related work on DED 15-5PH alloy demonstrates that prior thermal history governs attainable martensite and austenite fractions and shifts the precipitation response (Ref  20 ). For AISI Type 431 specifically, reported heat-treatment investigations predominantly involve austenitization or solution treatment prior to tempering, or address alloy variants and deposition geometries that do not represent as-deposited DED-LB multilayer conditions (Ref  7 ,  8 - 9 ,  21 ). The role of austenite reversion and matrix recovery during direct tempering from the as-deposited state remains poorly understood, and the processing–structure–property response for this route is insufficiently defined.

This work establishes a single-step isothermal tempering map for DED-LB AISI Type 431 across 350-650 °C, applied directly from the as-deposited state without prior austenitization. Phase fractions and lattice strain are quantified and correlated with room-temperature mechanical properties measured along the build direction. Results are benchmarked against commercial wrought AISI type 431 form. The study aims to identify practical tempering regimes for direct post-deposition property control, clarify the competing roles of austenite reversion and matrix recovery in governing ductility, and demonstrate a simplified thermal processing route applicable to repair and near-net-shape AM of martensitic stainless steels.

sections.heading: Powder Feedstock
paragraphs: A commercial water-atomized AISI Type 431 stainless-steel powder (nominal size range 45-125 µm) was used for DED-LB. Feedstock composition is listed in Table  1  based on supplier certificate of analysis and falls within typical AISI Type 431 limits for wrought product standards (e.g., ASTM A276). Table 1 Certificate of Analysis (CoA) chemistry for the water-atomized AISI 431 powder feedstock (wt.%) Powder feedstock Chemical Composition (wt.%) Fe C Si Cr Ni P S Others a AISI type 431 stainless steel Bal. 0.205 0.64 16.25 1.86 0.001 0.007 … a Denotes minor alloying or residual elements not individually listed on the certificate.

Powder morphology was examined by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess particle shape and surface condition (Fig.  1 ). The water-atomized feedstock was selected because it confirmed a higher coupling efficiency (laser absorptance) than gas-atomized powder of the same alloy in prior work (Ref  22 ). Fig. 1 SEM image showing morphology of the water-atomized AISI 431 powder feedstock

Particle size distribution (PSD) was measured by laser diffraction in accordance with ASTM B822. Differential and cumulative distributions, together with D10, D50, and D90 diameters, are shown in Fig.  2 . Observed deviations from the nominal sieve band are attributed to orientation bias during commercial sieving (e.g., admission of elongated/plate-like particles) and known laser-diffraction limitations for non-spherical morphologies. Fig. 2 Particle size distribution of the powder feedstock measured by laser diffraction in accordance with ASTM B822 (differential and cumulative distributions shown)

Bulk powder handling characteristics were measured using Hall flowmeter methods. Apparent density was measured in accordance with ASTM B212 and flow rate in accordance with ASTM B213. PSD and bulk powder results are summarized in Table  2 . Table 2 Water-atomized AISI 431 powder feedstock characteristics Parameter Value Unit Particle size, D10 a 64 µm Particle size, D50 a 110 µm Particle size, D90 a 187 µm Apparent density, Hall b 3.35 g/cm 3 Flow rate, Hall b 28.6 s/50 g a D10, D50, and D90 measured by laser diffraction in accordance with ASTM B822. b Apparent density and Hall flow rate measured in accordance with ASTM B212 and ASTM B213.

sections.heading: Processing
paragraphs: Deposition was performed on an automated industrial DED-LB platform equipped with a near-infrared diode laser ( λ  = 900-1080 nm) and integrated motion control. The system was operated in an off-axis configuration with the laser beam inclined 20-30° relative to the vertical powder in-feed. The substrate was an ASTM A36 carbon-steel plate (25 mm thick). The substrate surface was wire brushed, cleaned with acetone, and preheated by oxy-fuel heating to 150 °C prior to deposition. A multi-layer wall was produced by overlapping adjacent tracks to form a layer and repeating layers at constant nozzle–workpiece standoff (Fig.  3 ) to achieve final dimensions ≥ 120 × 20 × 60 mm. Fig. 3 Off-axis DED-LB deposition strategy for the multilayer wall build. Tracks are overlapped to form a layer, and layers are repeated at constant nozzle–workpiece standoff. All dimensions in mm

Main processing parameters are established from an industrial process window and are summarized in Table  3 . During deposition, nitrogen (7 SLPM) was used as the powder carrier gas, and the melt pool was shielded by a mixed flow of helium (5 SLPM) and argon (5 SLPM). The parameter set yielded a consistent layer height of approximately 1 mm. Table 3 Primary DED-LB processing parameters Parameter a Value Unit P  – Laser Power 3000 W V  – Velocity 1500 mm/min d spot  – Spot size (diam.) 4.8 mm M  – Mass flow rate 30 g/min S  – Hatch spacing 2 mm a Parameter definitions follow Martukanitz (Ref  23 ).

sections.heading: Tempering
paragraphs: After deposition, the deposited wall was separated from the substrate and face-machined to achieve a smooth, square finish. Five coupons were sectioned longitudinally to the build direction using wire electron discharge machining (EDM) and finish-machined to 20 × 10 × 55 mm (Fig.  4 ). Fig. 4 Coupon sectioning layout for tempering samples extracted from the DED-LB wall. All dimensions in mm

One coupon was retained in the as-deposited condition. The other four coupons were single tempered at 350, 450, 550, and 650 °C. Tempering was performed isothermally in a non-pressurized tube furnace (MTI OTF-1200X) under a continuous, low argon purge delivered via a tubelet at one end; the opposite end was vented to atmosphere via a needle valve to prevent pressurization (Fig.  5 a). Prior to heating, coupons were wrapped in stainless-steel foil to minimize surface reactions (Fig.  5 b). Each coupon was inserted only after the furnace reached the set temperature, held at temperature for 120 min, then removed, air-cooled to room temperature, and unwrapped. Figure  5 (c) shows the temper colors for each condition relative to the as-deposited, machined coupon. Fig. 5 Tempering setup and surface appearance after single tempering: (a) tube furnace with argon purge; (b) coupon wrapped in stainless-steel foil; (c) surface temper colors after tempering at 350-650 °C

sections.heading: Characterization and Analysis
paragraphs: Each coupon was sectioned by wire EDM to produce three miniaturized flat tensile specimens and three 10 × 10 mm surface specimens for microstructural examination and hardness testing (Fig.  6 ). Surface specimens were prepared by wet SiC grinding (P320, P600, P1200), diamond polishing (9 µm, 3 µm), and final chemical–mechanical polishing with colloidal silica (OP-S), with thorough cleaning and drying between steps. After final polishing, selected surfaces were etched in aqua regia diluted with 20% water for 10 s, then rinsed, cleaned, and dried prior to imaging. Etched microstructures were imaged using an optical microscope (Olympus BX53M) equipped with a digital camera (Olympus SC50) in bright field. Microstructure was also examined using a Zeiss Merlin field emission scanning electron microscope (FEG-SEM). Elemental analysis of surface features was performed by energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) using an Oxford Instruments X-MaxN silicon drift detector at 15 kV to identify inclusion chemistry. Tensile specimens were mechanically finished post-EDM to remove the recast layer and obtain a smooth, burr-free gauge. Benchmark specimens of identical geometry were extracted from a wrought AISI 431 bar (Ø 69.85 mm [2¾ in]) supplied to AS 1444-2007 Condition T; the bar was single austenitized at 980 °C and single tempered at 700 °C prior to extraction. Fig. 6 Specimen extraction layout from a tempering coupon showing locations and orientations of (i) miniaturized tensile specimens and (ii) 10 × 10 mm surface specimens for microstructure, XRD, EBSD, and hardness

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed using an Oxford Instruments AZtecHKL system at 70° tilt. Maps covered approximately 100 × 75 µm using a 0.10-µm step size (1000 × 750 points) at 20 kV. Patterns were collected using a Symmetry detector (156 × 128 pixels, Speed-2) with 1.0 ms exposure. Indexing used the Tru-I Hough-based solver (Hough 90; 11 bands). Enabled phases were Fe-BCC (space group 229,  a  = 2.866 Å) and Fe-FCC (space group 225,  a  = 3.6599 Å). Data were filtered using CI ≥ 0.1, and field coverage exceeded 85% for all maps.

Geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density was estimated from EBSD lattice curvature (Nye tensor) using Fe-BCC pixels only. A 5 × 5 kernel (effective window 0.50 µm) was used with a maximum neighbor misorientation of 5°. Dislocation character was decomposed using a weighted Burgers-vector basis assuming ½〈111〉 for BCC, with  α  = 3. Mean and standard deviation GND values were calculated from consistent regions of interest using identical acquisition and processing settings and are reported as a lower-bound estimate. Values of Kernel Average Misorientation (KAM) and mean angular deviation (MAD) were also obtained. These EBSD metrics are used strictly as proxies for stored microstructural strain/lattice distortion at the grain and sub-grain scale (Type II/III) in this study, and not as a measure of macroscopic (Type I) residual stress.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed on surface specimens using a Malvern Panalytical Empyrean  θ - θ  diffractometer in reflection geometry with a reflection–transmission spinner stage (1 s revolution). A Cu LFF tube operated at 40 kV and 40 mA. Incident- and diffracted-beam optics and detector settings were as follows: Ni Kβ filter (0.020 mm), 0.04 rad Soller slits, 10 mm mask, fixed anti-scatter slit of 2°, programmable divergence slit set to 1°, and a PIXcel3D 1 × 1 area detector in scanning mode (PHD 25-70%). Continuous scans were acquired from 20 to 120° 2 θ  using a 0.005° step and 0.005° min −1  scan speed. Wavelengths were λKα1 = 1.540598 Å and λKα2 = 1.544426 Å (Kα2/Kα1 = 0.5); λKβ was suppressed. Patterns were refined using Profex v5.6.1 (BGMN) with a fundamental-parameters instrument profile. The refinement model included phase scale factors, unit-cell parameters, global zero/sample displacement, background, and where required peak-shape, crystallite size, and microstrain. Preferred orientation was treated using spherical harmonics. Phase identification used the ICDD PDF-5 + database.

Vickers hardness (HV5) was measured using a Nanovea CB500 tester with a Vickers indenter. A 3 × 3 indentation matrix at 1 mm pitch was applied using a 5-kgf load and a 10-s dwell. Vickers hardness was calculated from mean diagonal length in accordance with ASTM E92. Indents satisfied minimum spacing criteria (≥3 × diagonal between centers and ≥ 2.5 × diagonal to edges for steels). Hardness is reported as mean ± standard deviation from nine indents per condition.

Uniaxial tensile tests were performed at ambient temperature using an MTS Exceed E44 system under digital closed-loop control. The engineering strain rate was 2.5 × 10 − 4  s − 1 . Strain was measured using a non-contact MTS Advantage video extensometer (XT-102) calibrated to ASTM E83 (Class B-1). Miniaturized flat tensile specimens were extracted along the build direction (BD), as shown in Fig.  6 . Load and strain were recorded at 20 Hz. Yield strength (0.2% offset), ultimate tensile strength, and elongation were determined in accordance with ASTM E8/E8M. Tensile properties are reported as mean ± standard deviation from three specimens per condition.

The BD was selected as the primary test orientation based on its relevance to structural loading in powder-fed DED-LB components and its representation of the lower-bound ductility response in the build. Preliminary tensile data obtained along the scanning direction (SD) from a separately deposited block under equivalent processing conditions showed marginally higher elongation than BD, consistent with reported anisotropy in DED-LB martensitic steels (Ref  12 ,  24 ). Hardness and tensile SD data for the as-deposited condition are included in the results section for reference only.

Fracture surface morphology was examined by SEM on tensile fracture specimens without preparation, using secondary electron imaging at 10 kV. EDS elemental maps were collected at 15 kV with sufficient integration time to ensure adequate signal-to-noise for inclusion chemistry identification.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs: Figure  7  shows the as-deposited DED-LB microstructure of AISI 431. The matrix is lath martensite containing a cellular solidification substructure, with discrete δ-ferrite pockets located between martensite domains. The areal fraction of observed δ-ferrite is estimated to be approximately 10-12%, with locally higher concentrations occurring near interlayer overlap regions. Both the morphology and the estimated δ-ferrite content are consistent with prior reports on laser-deposited 431-type martensitic stainless steels (Ref  7 ,  9 ). Fig. 7 As-deposited AISI 431 DED-LB microstructure showing lath martensite (M) with cellular substructure and δ-ferrite pockets ( δ ). BD and LD are indicated. Bright-field optical micrograph. Etched in aqua regia diluted with 20% water for 10 s

The phase constitution is expected for the Cr-rich, Ni-lean 431 composition. The WRC-1992 constitution diagram places this chemistry in the primary-δ or ferrite–austenite (FA) solidification fields, indicating δ-ferrite as the primary solidification phase followed by γ-austenite formation during cooling (Ref  25 ). On further cooling through M s ,  γ  transforms to lath martensite. The short thermal cycles and high-temperature exposure associated with laser deposition limit  δ  →  γ  transformation, resulting in a higher retained δ-ferrite fraction at room temperature than found in conventional forms.

Further SEM examination revealed dispersed, near-circular pits, some containing spherical non-conductive particles (Fig.  8 a). The pits are up to ~ 10 µm in diameter, although most are ≤ 1 µm. EDS spot and map analyses indicate that the particles are Si-Mn-rich oxide inclusions. Elevated Si and Mn signals were also detected at open pits where particles were absent (Fig.  8 c), consistent with particle pullout during metallographic preparation. Similar spherical oxide features with comparable Si-Mn enrichment were subsequently identified within the water-atomized powder feedstock (Fig.  8 b), indicating that these inclusions were inherited from powder manufacture rather than formed in situ during DED-LB processing. This interpretation aligns with prior studies reporting Mn-Si-(Cr)-rich oxide particulates and higher oxide coverage associated with water-atomized stainless-steel powders (Ref  27 ,  28 ) as well as evidence that oxide inclusions present in precursor powders can persist into stainless steel additively manufactured microstructures (Ref  29 ,  30 ). Fig. 8 Si-Mn-rich oxide inclusions and associated pull-out pits. (a) SEM of polished DED-LB deposit showing round pullout pits, some containing spherical non-conductive particles. (b) Similar inclusions embedded in the powder feedstock. (c) EDS showing Si-Mn enrichment at inclusions and/or pits

Tempering effects were evaluated by EBSD. Figure  9  shows representative EBSD datasets for the as-deposited condition, the 350 °C and 650 °C single-tempered conditions, and the wrought Condition T reference (complete datasets for all conditions are provided in the Supplementary Material). Across all DED-LB conditions, the microstructure remains predominantly a BCC lath-martensitic matrix containing discrete δ-ferrite islands. δ-ferrite retains a single crystallographic orientation within each island, while the surrounding martensite shows packet/block orientation variation. In the as-deposited condition, the martensitic orientation field is more heterogeneous, consistent with a high defect density and fine sub-lath boundary structure produced by rapid cooling and repeated thermal cycling. Fig. 9 EBSD maps for AISI 431: as-deposited DED-LB, single-tempered at 350 °C, single-tempered at 650 °C, and wrought Condition T reference. Left: BC + IPF + GB maps. Right: KAM + phase boundary maps. Additional EBSD datasets are provided in the Supplementary Material

With increasing tempering temperature, the martensitic orientation field becomes more uniform and boundaries become less fragmented, indicating recovery and sub-lath boundary relaxation. By 650 °C, the martensitic orientation field shows the strongest preferred orientation among the DED-LB conditions, consistent with recovery and partial coarsening of lath blocks. The wrought reference exhibits a coarser tempered morphology and a larger δ-ferrite region, reflecting homogenization and high-temperature tempering in conventional bar processing.

KAM maps show that local misorientation is concentrated in martensitic regions and is negligible in δ-ferrite. This distribution reflects the transformation-induced dislocation structure of martensite and the absence of transformation shear strain in δ-ferrite. The same trend is captured by GND estimates derived from EBSD curvature analysis (Supplementary Material).

MAD decreases from 0.64 ± 0.20° in the as-deposited state to 0.33 ± 0.21° after tempering at 650 °C. The wrought Condition-T reference shows MAD of 0.46 ± 0.21°. The reduction in MAD with tempering indicates progressive removal of stored strain through recovery and dislocation annihilation. In this dataset, the 650 °C condition shows lower MAD than the wrought reference, indicating that high-temperature tempering is sufficient to reduce transformation-induced strain to a level comparable to, and below, the conventional benchmark.

A distinguishing feature of the 350 °C condition is the appearance of FCC phase boundaries, concentrated at δ-ferrite/martensite interfaces as observed in Fig.  9  KAM + PB maps. This indicates early-stage austenite reversion during low-temperature tempering. Carbon partitioning to high-energy boundaries, particularly  δ / α ′ interfaces, can stabilize thin reverted-austenite films or pockets. These films often maintain Kurdjumov–Sachs or Nishiyama–Wassermann orientation relationships with adjacent BCC phases, allowing EBSD detection even at low volume fraction (Ref  31 ,  32 ,  33 - 34 ).

XRD with Rietveld refinement was used for quantitative phase assessment. Figure  10  shows representative refinement for the as-deposited condition, with indexed BCC and FCC reflections. Refinement statistics for all conditions are provided in the Supplementary material. Fig. 10 Representative Rietveld refinement for the as-deposited DED-LB AISI 431 condition showing observed and calculated profiles, difference curve, and indexed BCC and FCC reflections

Diffraction patterns in Fig.  11  show an increase in FCC peak intensity after tempering at 350 °C and a reduction at 450 °C. FCC peaks are not detected after tempering at 550 °C and 650 °C. The wrought reference similarly shows no distinguishable FCC peaks at the measurement sensitivity. The progressive sharpening of BCC reflections with increasing tempering temperature indicates reduction of defect-related broadening consistent with recovery. Fig. 11 XRD patterns for DED-LB AISI 431 in the as-deposited and single-tempered conditions (350-650 °C) and for the wrought Condition-T reference

EBSD confirms the spatial distribution of austenite in the 350 °C condition (Fig.  12 ). Austenite forms as thin interfacial films adjacent to δ-ferrite pockets, consistent with interface-assisted nucleation driven by local carbon enrichment at  δ / α ′ boundaries (Ref  35 ). Fig. 12 EBSD phase map with band contrast for the 350 °C single-tempered condition showing reverted/retained austenite adjacent to δ-ferrite pockets

Rietveld-derived austenite fractions (retained + reverted) are summarized in Fig.  13 . Austenite increases from 3.86 ± 0.95% in the as-deposited condition to 6.68 ± 0.98% after tempering at 350 °C, consistent with low-temperature reversion. At 450 °C, austenite decreases to 4.28 ± 0.51%, consistent with reduced FCC peak intensity and competing recovery/precipitation processes. At 550 °C and 650 °C, austenite falls below 1%, indicating a fully tempered martensitic matrix. The wrought Condition T reference also contains < 1% austenite. Fig. 13 Austenite volume fraction (retained + reverted) from Rietveld refinement for the DED-LB as-deposited and tempering series

Overall, the EBSD and XRD datasets define a low-temperature reversion regime centered near 350 °C and a high-temperature regime (>550 °C) where austenite is suppressed and recovery dominates. In contrast to Cu-bearing AM AISI Type 431 variants where austenite stability can persist to higher tempering temperatures, the present alloy shows reversion confined to the low-temperature window (Ref  21 ).

sections.heading: Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: Figure  14  shows room-temperature engineering stress–strain curves for all DED-LB conditions and the wrought reference. The as-deposited material fails at maximum load with negligible uniform strain (≈1.2%) and no observable necking, indicating limited plasticity and low work-hardening capacity. This response reflects a supersaturated lath-martensitic matrix with high stored strain and strong local constraint associated with the as-deposited microstructure. In the as-built condition, tensile properties were comparable between SD and BD orientations, with ductility marginally higher along SD. Fig. 14 Room-temperature engineering stress–strain curves for AISI Type 431: DED-LB specimens (as-deposited and single-step tempered at 350-650 °C) and a wrought reference (AS 1444-2007, Condition T)

Tempering at 350 °C increases elongation to ≈10.2% while retaining high strength (UTS 1180 MPa compared with 1235 MPa as-deposited). The curve shows stable plastic flow and clear necking, indicating restored deformation capacity. The improvement is attributed to partial recovery combined with interfacial reverted/retained austenite, which delays strain localization without requiring a large reduction in flow stress.

Tempering at 450 °C reduces elongation to 3.6% while slightly increasing strength (UTS 1227 MPa). This response coincides with peak hardness (Fig.  15 ) and reduced FCC fraction, consistent with secondary hardening and reduced austenite contribution. The reduced ductility indicates earlier strain localization in a strengthened matrix with limited strain accommodation. Fig. 15 Effect of single tempering temperature (350-650 °C, 2 h) on DED-LB AISI 431 mechanical properties: ultimate tensile strength, 0.2% yield strength, elongation, and HV5 hardness

At 550 °C, strength decreases to 994 MPa while elongation increases to 12.6%, indicating transition to a fully tempered martensitic matrix dominated by recovery and sub-lath coarsening. At 650 °C, strength decreases to 821 MPa and elongation increases further to ≈19.7%, reaching and marginally exceeding the elongation of the wrought reference (17.4%). In this regime, curve shape indicates improved strain-hardening stability and reduced sensitivity to local microstructural heterogeneity.

Figure  15  summarizes strength, elongation, and hardness trends across the tempering series. Secondary hardening is centered near 450 °C and is reflected by the hardness peak of 606 HV. Above 500 °C, strength and hardness decrease markedly while ductility increases. Elongation at 350 °C shows the largest scatter, which indicates that low-temperature tempering improves mean ductility but does not fully homogenize build-induced variability. At higher tempering temperatures, recovery reduces stored strain and the scatter decreases as deformation response becomes more uniform across the gauge length.

From a heat-treatment selection perspective, the results define three operating windows. Tempering near 350 °C provides high strength with a large ductility increase but higher scatter. Tempering near 450 °C maximizes hardness and strength through secondary hardening but reduces ductility. Tempering at ≥ 550 °C gives reproducible ductility with reduced strength, and 650 °C provides wrought-like elongation. These windows support component-level selection where 350-450 °C suits strength-limited applications with controlled strain demand, while ≥ 550 °C suits applications that require ductility and stability.

Table  4  benchmarks the present DED-LB AISI 431 results against published mechanical property ranges for the same alloy produced by alternative processing routes and post-weld/heat-treatment schedules. Literature DED-LB data for AISI Type 431 show that properties depend strongly on whether austenitization is performed prior to tempering. Routes that include austenitization prior to tempering typically homogenize segregation, dissolve preexisting carbides, and reform martensite on quenching, which increases the attainable strength after tempering but can reduce the contribution of interface-stabilized austenite and therefore limit ductility gains at low tempering temperatures. In contrast, the present direct-tempered DED-LB route starts from an as-deposited martensitic substructure with high defect density and residual strain, which explains the very high as-deposited strength together with low elongation, and it also explains why modest thermal exposure at 350 °C can produce a large ductility increase: Interfacial reverted/retained austenite forms at δ-ferrite/martensite boundaries and provides local strain accommodation without requiring a full microstructural reset. The secondary-hardening response at 450 °C aligns with literature tempering behavior in martensitic stainless steels, where strengthening processes outpace recovery and reduce strain accommodation, while the convergence toward wrought-like ductility at ≥ 650 °C reflects recovery-dominated tempering that reduces stored strain and microstructural heterogeneity regardless of whether the starting state was deposited or welded. Welding-based datasets fall between these bounds because weld thermal cycles create martensitic regions with high stored strain and heterogeneous microstructures, and post-weld austenitize-and-temper schedules move the response toward the conventional wrought envelope by reducing heterogeneity and stabilizing the tempered martensitic matrix. sections.heading: Fractography
paragraphs: Figure  16  compares representative fracture surfaces of the DED-LB as-deposited and ST 650 °C conditions and the wrought reference material. The as-deposited condition exhibits a predominantly quasi-cleavage fracture morphology, characterized by small, poorly defined cleavage facets interconnected by shallow dimples, reflecting the simultaneous operation of cleavage and localized plasticity at the crack tip. At the macroscopic scale, the gauge-section geometry remains largely unchanged, confirming negligible plastic deformation prior to failure. This behavior is consistent with brittle fracture of a supersaturated, highly strained martensitic matrix, in which elevated dislocation density and transformation strain severely restrict strain accommodation. Crack initiation in this condition is dominated by Si-Mn-rich oxide inclusions, which act as stress concentrators in a matrix incapable of local plastic redistribution, as discussed further below. Fig. 16 SEM fracture surfaces of AISI Type 431: (a,b) DED-LB as-deposited; (c,d) DED-LB ST 650 °C; (e,f) wrought Condition T. Yellow arrows indicate Si-Mn-rich oxide inclusions; green arrow marks a ferrite stringer fracture site

Following tempering at 650 °C, the fracture surface becomes markedly more tortuous and irregular, with a clear transition toward dimple-dominated microvoid coalescence. The dimples are more uniformly distributed, reflecting enhanced void nucleation and growth enabled by matrix recovery. Fracture proceeds predominantly by a transgranular mechanism throughout, consistent with the tempered martensitic microstructure. This fractographic evolution is fully consistent with the recovered and tempered martensitic microstructure and the measured tensile elongation of 19.7%. In contrast, the wrought reference material (elongation of 17.4%) exhibits well-developed dimple rupture, with discernible alignment reflecting the prior rolling direction, confirming classical ductile fracture behavior. Localized intergranular fracture features were occasionally observed in the wrought condition, associated with ferrite stringers or residual ferritic regions inherited from the rolling process.

All DED-LB conditions reveal a persistent population of Si-Mn-rich oxide micro-inclusions, previously identified in Fig.  8 . In the as-deposited condition, these inclusions typically retain their spherical morphology at fracture, consistent with their brittle, non-deforming character during rapid crack propagation. In conditions exhibiting greater tensile elongation, particularly following tempering at 650 °C, extensive inclusion cracking and fragmentation is observed, indicating that the inclusions are subjected to significant mechanical loading prior to final fracture. EDS analysis confirms consistent inclusion chemistry across all conditions, exemplified by the ST 650 °C condition in Fig.  17 , where fragmented particles exhibit Si, Mn, O, and minor Cr signals. Despite the persistence of this inclusion population, bulk ductility increases substantially—from 1.2% in the as-deposited state to 19.7% after tempering at 650 °C—demonstrating that inclusion content alone does not govern the observed ductility evolution induced by tempering. Fig. 17 EDS elemental maps of Si-Mn-rich oxide inclusions on the DED-LB AISI Type 431 ST 650 °C fracture surface

In the supersaturated as-deposited martensitic matrix, oxide inclusions act as highly effective crack-initiation sites because the surrounding matrix lacks the capacity for local plastic stress redistribution. Following high-temperature tempering, the same inclusion population is more effectively accommodated, as matrix recovery enables plastic constraint and strain redistribution around the particles prior to void coalescence and final fracture. It is important to distinguish between inclusion  content —which remains fixed across all conditions—and inclusion  behavior , which is strongly dependent on the surrounding matrix state. Matrix recovery driven by tempering, therefore, emerges as the dominant mechanism controlling ductility progression across the tempering series. While tempering does not eliminate the feedstock-inherited inclusion content, the fixed number density and chemistry of the Si-Mn-rich oxides impose an upper bound on achievable tensile ductility that cannot be overcome by heat-treatment selection alone, and dedicated fracture toughness testing would be required to quantify their influence on crack propagation resistance.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This work demonstrates that direct single-step tempering, without austenitization, provides a practical and component-scalable route to stabilize and tailor the mechanical response of DED-LB AISI Type 431 stainless steel. Tempering temperature functions as a tuning parameter that moves the deposit between three operationally distinct performance regimes: a low-temperature regime (350 °C) restores useful ductility while largely retaining high strength; an intermediate regime (450 °C) prioritizes peak secondary hardening at the expense of strain accommodation; and a high-temperature regime (≥550 °C) emphasizes martensitic recovery, strain relief, and deformation stability. The practical significance of this ductility recovery is substantial. Elongation increases from 1.2% in the as-deposited condition to 10.2% following low-temperature tempering, and reaches 19.7% at the high-temperature end, approaching the elongation of the wrought reference material.

Mechanistically, two complementary processes underpin this progression. In the low-temperature regime, interface-assisted austenite reversion at δ-ferrite/martensite boundaries contributes to ductility recovery, identifying the δ-ferrite network topology as an intrinsic microstructural parameter capable of influencing the ductility response in additively manufactured 431 alloy. At higher tempering temperatures, progressive reduction of martensitic-stored strain becomes the dominant contribution, yielding improved yield stability, reduced sensitivity to process-induced microstructural variability, and enhanced residual-stress and dimensional stability during post-processing. Si-Mn-rich oxide inclusions inherited from the water-atomized feedstock were identified as crack-initiation sites. However, their influence is matrix-state dependent. In the supersaturated as-deposited condition, they are highly detrimental, whereas following matrix recovery they are more effectively accommodated through local plastic constraint. Tempering-driven matrix recovery, rather than any change in inclusion content or chemistry, is therefore the dominant mechanism governing ductility progression across the tempering series. The fixed inclusion population imposes an upper bound on tensile ductility that is independent of heat-treatment selection.

Overall, these findings provide a systematic, single-step heat-treatment framework for DED-LB 431, enabling informed post-processing selection based on whether the application is strength-limited, hardness-limited, or ductility- and stability-limited. Future work should address the quantitative influence of the Si-Mn-rich inclusion population on fracture toughness. In parallel, feedstock modification or in-process parameter control should be examined as potential routes to reducing inclusion number density and further extending the achievable property envelope.
